Read this before adding a new slash command that coordinates multiple personas, or before introducing a new persona that \\\"wraps\\\" existing ones.\\n\\nThe governing rule: **the user (or a slash command) is the orchestrator. Personas do not invoke other personas.** Skills are mandatory hops inside a persona's workflow.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Endorsed patterns\\n\\n### 1. Direct invocation (no orchestration)\\n\\nSingle persona, single perspective, single artifact. The default and the cheapest option.\\n\\n```\\nuser → code-reviewer → report → user\\n```\\n\\n**Use when:** the work is one perspective on one artifact and you can describe it in one sentence.\\n\\n**Examples:**\\n- \\\"Review this PR\\\" → `code-reviewer`\\n- \\\"Find security issues in `auth.ts`\\\" → `security-auditor`\\n- \\\"What tests are missing for the checkout flow?\\\" → `test-engineer`\\n\\n**Cost:** one round trip. The baseline you should always compare orchestrated patterns against.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 2. Single-persona slash command\\n\\nA slash command that wraps one persona with the project's skills. Saves the user from re-explaining the workflow every time.\\n\\n```\\n/review → code-reviewer (with code-review-and-quality skill) → report\\n```\\n\\n**Use when:** the same single-persona invocation happens repeatedly with the same setup.\\n\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/review`, `/test`, `/code-simplify`.\\n\\n**Cost:** same as direct invocation. The slash command is just a saved prompt.\\n\\n**Anti-signal:** if the slash command's body is mostly \\\"decide which persona to call,\\\" delete it and let the user call the persona directly.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 3. Parallel fan-out with merge\\n\\nMultiple personas operate on the same input concurrently, each producing an independent report. A merge step (in the main agent's context) synthesizes them into a single decision.\\n\\n```\\n                    ┌─→ code-reviewer    ─┐\\n/ship → fan out  ───┼─→ security-auditor ─┤→ merge → go/no-go + rollback\\n                    └─→ test-engineer    ─┘\\n```\\n\\n**Use when:**\\n- The sub-tasks are genuinely independent (no shared mutable state, no ordering dependency)\\n- Each sub-agent benefits from its own context window\\n- The merge step is small enough to stay in the main context\\n- Wall-clock latency matters\\n\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/ship`.\\n\\n**Cost:** N parallel sub-agent contexts + one merge turn. Higher than direct invocation, but faster wall-clock and produces better reports because each sub-agent stays focused on its single perspective.\\n\\n**Validation checklist before adopting this pattern:**\\n- [ ] Can I run all sub-agents at the same time without ordering issues?\\n- [ ] Does each persona produce a different *kind* of finding, not just the same finding from a different angle?\\n- [ ] Will the merge step fit in the main agent's remaining context?\\n- [ ] Is the user's wait time long enough that parallelism is actually noticeable?\\n\\nIf any answer is \\\"no,\\\" fall back to direct invocation or a single-persona command.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 4. Sequential pipeline as user-driven slash commands\\n\\nThe user runs slash commands in a defined order, carrying context (or commit history) between them. There is no orchestrator agent — the user IS the orchestrator.\\n\\n```\\nuser runs:  /spec  →  /plan  →  /build  →  /test  →  /review  →  /ship\\n```\\n\\n**Use when:** the workflow has dependencies (each step needs the previous step's output) and human judgment between steps adds value.\\n\\n**Examples in this repo:** the entire DEFINE → PLAN → BUILD → VERIFY → REVIEW → SHIP lifecycle.\\n\\n**Cost:** one sub-agent context per step. Free for the orchestration layer because there is no orchestrator agent.\\n\\n**Why not automate it:** an LLM \\\"lifecycle orchestrator\\\" would (a) lose nuance between steps because it has to summarize for hand-off, (b) skip the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work early, and (c) double the token cost via paraphrasing turns.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 5. Research isolation (context preservation)\\n\\nWhen a task requires reading large amounts of material that shouldn't pollute the main context, spawn a research sub-agent that returns only a digest.\\n\\n```\\nmain agent → research sub-agent (reads 50 files) → digest → main agent continues\\n```\\n\\n**Use when:**\\n- The main session needs to stay focused on a downstream task\\n- The investigation result is much smaller than the input it consumes\\n- The decision quality benefits from the main agent having room to think after\\n\\n**Examples:** \\\"Find every call site of this deprecated API across the monorepo,\\\" \\\"Summarize what these 30 ADRs say about caching.\\\"\\n\\n**Cost:** one isolated sub-agent context. Worth it any time the alternative is loading hundreds of files into the main context.\\n\\n**On Claude Code, use the built-in `Explore` subagent** rather than defining a custom research persona. `Explore` runs on Haiku, is denied write/edit tools, and is purpose-built for this pattern. Define a custom research subagent only when `Explore` doesn't fit (e.g. you need a domain-specific system prompt the model wouldn't infer).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Claude Code compatibility\\n\\nThis catalog is harness-agnostic, but most readers will run it on Claude Code. Here's how each pattern maps onto Claude Code's primitives — and where the platform enforces our rules for us.\\n\\n### Where personas live\\n\\nPlugin subagents go in `agents/` at the plugin root. This repo is a plugin (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`), so `agents/code-reviewer.md`, `agents/security-auditor.md`, and `agents/test-engineer.md` are auto-discovered when the plugin is enabled. No path configuration needed.\\n\\n### Subagents vs. Agent Teams\\n\\nClaude Code has two parallelism primitives. Pattern 3 (parallel fan-out with merge) maps to **subagents**. If you need teammates that talk to each other, use **Agent Teams** instead.\\n\\n| | Subagents | Agent Teams |\\n|--|-----------|-------------|\\n| Coordination | Main agent fans out, sub-agents only report back | Teammates message each other, share a task list |\\n| Context | Own context window per subagent | Own context window per teammate |\\n| When to use | Independent tasks producing reports | Collaborative work needing discussion |\\n| Status | Stable | Experimental — requires `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` |\\n| Cost | Lower | Higher — each teammate is a separate Claude instance |\\n\\n**The personas in this repo work in both modes.** When spawned as subagents (e.g. by `/ship`), they report findings to the main session. When spawned as teammates (`Spawn a teammate using the security-auditor agent type…`), they can challenge each other's findings directly. The persona definition is the same; only the spawning context changes.\\n\\nOne subtlety: the `skills` and `mcpServers` frontmatter fields in a persona are honored when it runs as a subagent but **ignored when it runs as a teammate** — teammates load skills and MCP servers from your project and user settings, the same as a regular session. If a persona depends on a specific skill or MCP server being loaded, configure it at the session level so it's available in both modes.\\n\\n### Platform-enforced rules\\n\\nTwo rules in this catalog aren't just convention — Claude Code enforces them:\\n\\n- **\\\"Subagents cannot spawn other subagents\\\"** (verbatim from the docs). Anti-pattern B (persona-calls-persona) and Anti-pattern D (deep persona trees) cannot exist on Claude Code by construction.\\n- **\\\"No nested teams\\\"** — teammates cannot spawn their own teams. Same anti-patterns blocked at the team level.\\n\\nThis means you can adopt the patterns in this catalog without worrying about contributors accidentally building the anti-patterns. They'll just fail to load.\\n\\n### Built-in subagents to know about\\n\\nBefore defining a custom subagent, check whether one of these covers the role:\\n\\n| Built-in | Purpose |\\n|----------|---------|\\n| `Explore` | Read-only codebase search and analysis. Use this for Pattern 5 (research isolation). |\\n| `Plan` | Read-only research during plan mode. |\\n| `general-purpose` | Multi-step tasks needing both exploration and modification. |\\n\\nDon't redefine these. Layer your specialist personas (code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-engineer) on top of them.\\n\\n### Frontmatter restrictions for plugin agents\\n\\nPlugin subagents do **not** support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields — these are silently ignored. If a future persona needs any of those, the user must copy the file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` instead.\\n\\nThe fields that DO work in plugin agents are: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `memory`, `background`, `effort`, `isolation`, `color`, `initialPrompt`. Use `model` per-persona if you want to optimize cost (e.g. Haiku for `test-engineer` coverage scans, Sonnet for `code-reviewer`, Opus for `security-auditor`).\\n\\n### Spawning multiple subagents in parallel\\n\\nIn Claude Code, parallel fan-out (Pattern 3) requires issuing **multiple Agent tool calls in a single assistant turn**. Sequential turns serialize execution. `/ship` calls this out explicitly. Any new orchestrator command should do the same.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Worked example: Agent Teams for competing-hypothesis debugging\\n\\nThis example shows when to reach for **Agent Teams** instead of `/ship`'s subagent fan-out. The two patterns look similar from a distance — both spawn the same three personas — but the value comes from a different place.\\n\\n### The scenario\\n\\n> *Checkout occasionally hangs for ~30 seconds before completing. It happens roughly once every 50 sessions. No errors in logs. Started after last week's release.*\\n\\nPlausible root causes (mutually exclusive, all fit the symptoms):\\n\\n1. A race condition in the new payment-confirmation flow\\n2. An auth check that occasionally falls through to a slow synchronous network call\\n3. A missing index on a query that scales with cart size\\n4. A flaky third-party API where the SDK retries silently before timing out\\n\\nA single agent will pick the first plausible theory and stop investigating. A `/ship`-style subagent fan-out would have each persona report independently — but their reports never meet, so nothing rules out the wrong theories.\\n\\nThis is exactly the case the Agent Teams docs describe: *\\\"With multiple independent investigators actively trying to disprove each other, the theory that survives is much more likely to be the actual root cause.\\\"*\\n\\n### Why this is *not* a `/ship` job\\n\\n| | `/ship` (subagents) | Agent Teams |\\n|--|--------------------|-------------|\\n| Sub-agents see | The same diff, different lenses | A shared task list, each other's messages |\\n| Output | Three independent reports → one merge | Adversarial debate → consensus root cause |\\n| Right when | You want a verdict on a known artifact | You want to *find* the artifact among hypotheses |\\n\\n`/ship` is a verdict; Agent Teams is an investigation.\\n\\n### Setup (one-time, per-environment)\\n\\nAgent Teams is experimental. In `~/.claude/settings.json`:\\n\\n```json\\n{\\n  \\\"env\\\": {\\n    \\\"CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS\\\": \\\"1\\\"\\n  }\\n}\\n```\\n\\nRequires Claude Code v2.1.32 or later. The personas in this repo are picked up automatically — no team-config files to author by hand.\\n\\n### The trigger prompt\\n\\nType into the lead session, in natural language:\\n\\n```\\nUsers report checkout hangs for ~30 seconds intermittently after last\\nweek's release. No errors in logs.\\n\\nCreate an agent team to debug this with competing hypotheses. Spawn\\nthree teammates using the existing agent types:\\n\\n  - code-reviewer  — investigate race conditions and blocking calls\\n                     in the checkout code path\\n  - security-auditor — investigate auth checks, session handling,\\n                       and any synchronous network calls added recently\\n  - test-engineer  — propose tests that would distinguish between the\\n                     hypotheses and check coverage gaps in checkout\\n\\nHave them message each other directly to challenge each other's\\ntheories. Update findings as consensus emerges. Only converge when\\ntwo teammates agree they can disprove the others'.\\n```\\n\\nThe lead spawns three teammates referencing the existing persona names. The persona body is **appended** to each teammate's system prompt as additional instructions (on top of the team-coordination instructions the lead installs); the trigger prompt above becomes their task.\\n\\n### What happens\\n\\n1. Each teammate runs in its own context window, exploring the codebase from its own lens.\\n2. Teammates use `message` to send findings to each other directly. The lead doesn't have to relay.\\n3. The shared task list shows who's investigating what — visible at any time with `Ctrl+T` (in-process mode) or in a tmux pane (split mode).\\n4. When `code-reviewer` finds a `Promise.all` that should be sequential, it messages `security-auditor` to confirm the auth call isn't part of the race. `security-auditor` checks and replies — either confirming the race is the real issue or producing counter-evidence.\\n5. `test-engineer` proposes a focused integration test for whichever theory is winning, which the team uses to verify before declaring consensus.\\n6. The lead synthesizes the converged finding and presents it to you.\\n\\nYou can interrupt at any teammate by cycling with `Shift+Down` and typing — useful for redirecting an investigator who's gone down a wrong path.\\n\\n### When to clean up\\n\\nWhen the investigation lands on a root cause, tell the lead:\\n\\n```\\nClean up the team\\n```\\n\\nAlways cleanup through the lead, not a teammate (per the docs: teammates lack full team context for cleanup).\\n\\n### Cost expectation\\n\\nThree Sonnet teammates running for ~10–15 minutes of investigation costs noticeably more than the same three personas spawned as subagents by `/ship`. The justification is *quality of conclusion* — for production debugging where the wrong fix is expensive, the extra tokens are a bargain. For a routine PR review, stick with `/ship`.\\n\\n### Anti-pattern in this scenario\\n\\nDo **not** rebuild this as a `/debug` slash command that fans out subagents. Subagents can't message each other — you'd lose the adversarial debate that makes the pattern work. If a workflow keeps coming up, document the trigger prompt above as a snippet rather than wrapping it in a slash command that misuses subagents.\\n\\n### When *not* to use Agent Teams\\n\\n- Production-bound verdict on a known diff → use `/ship` (subagents).\\n- One specialist perspective on one artifact → direct persona invocation.\\n- Sequential lifecycle (spec → plan → build) → user-driven slash commands (Pattern 4).\\n- Read-heavy research with a small digest → built-in `Explore` subagent.\\n\\nReach for Agent Teams only when teammates **need** to challenge each other to produce the right answer.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Anti-patterns\\n\\n### A. Router persona (\\\"meta-orchestrator\\\")\\n\\nA persona whose job is to decide which other persona to call.\\n\\n```\\n/work → router-persona → \\\"this needs a review\\\" → code-reviewer → router (paraphrases) → user\\n```\\n\\n**Why it fails:**\\n- Pure routing layer with no domain value\\n- Adds two paraphrasing hops → information loss + roughly 2× token cost\\n- The user already knew they wanted a review; they could have called `/review` directly\\n- Replicates the work that slash commands and intent mapping in `AGENTS.md` already do\\n\\n**What to do instead:** add or refine slash commands. Document intent → command mapping in `AGENTS.md`.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### B. Persona that calls another persona\\n\\nA `code-reviewer` that internally invokes `security-auditor` when it sees auth code.\\n\\n**Why it fails:**\\n- Personas were designed to produce a single perspective; chaining them defeats that\\n- The summary the calling persona passes loses context the called persona needs\\n- Failure modes multiply (which persona's output format wins? whose rules apply?)\\n- Hides cost from the user\\n\\n**What to do instead:** have the calling persona *recommend* a follow-up audit in its report. The user or a slash command runs the second pass.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### C. Sequential orchestrator that paraphrases\\n\\nAn agent that calls `/spec`, then `/plan`, then `/build`, etc. on the user's behalf.\\n\\n**Why it fails:**\\n- Loses the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work\\n- Each hand-off summarizes context — accumulated drift over a long pipeline\\n- Doubles token cost: orchestrator turn + sub-agent turn for every step\\n- Removes user agency at exactly the points where judgment matters most\\n\\n**What to do instead:** keep the user as the orchestrator. Document the recommended sequence in `README.md` and let users invoke it.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### D. Deep persona trees\\n\\n`/ship` calls a `pre-ship-coordinator` that calls a `quality-coordinator` that calls `code-reviewer`.\\n\\n**Why it fails:**\\n- Each layer adds latency and tokens with no decision value\\n- Debugging becomes a multi-level investigation\\n- The leaf personas lose context to multiple summarization steps\\n\\n**What to do instead:** keep the orchestration depth at most 1 (slash command → personas). The merge happens in the main agent.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Decision flow\\n\\nWhen considering a new orchestrated workflow, walk this flow:\\n\\n```\\nIs the work one perspective on one artifact?\\n├── Yes → Direct invocation. Stop.\\n└── No  → Will the same composition repeat?\\n         ├── No  → Direct invocation, ad hoc. Stop.\\n         └── Yes → Are sub-tasks independent?\\n                  ├── No  → Sequential slash commands run by user (Pattern 4).\\n                  └── Yes → Parallel fan-out with merge (Pattern 3).\\n                           Validate against the checklist above.\\n                           If any check fails → fall back to single-persona command (Pattern 2).\\n```\\n\\n---\\n\\n## When to add a new pattern to this catalog\\n\\nAdd a new entry only after:\\n\\n1. You've used the pattern at least twice in real work\\n2. You can name a concrete artifact in this repo that demonstrates it\\n3. You can explain why an existing pattern wouldn't have worked\\n4. You can describe its anti-pattern shadow (what people will mistakenly build instead)\\n\\nPremature catalog entries become aspirational documentation that no one follows.\\n\",\n  \"encoding\": \"base64\",\n  \"_links\": {\n    \"self\": \"https://api.github.com/repos/addyosmani/agent-skills/contents/references/orchestration-patterns.md?ref=main\",\n    \"git\": \"https://api.github.com/repos/addyosmani/agent-skills/git/blobs/09cddd31d52a95be1d9bca814547d184b9945e44\",\n    \"html\": \"https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/blob/main/references/orchestration-patterns.md\"\n  }\n}"}],"structured_content":null},"error":null,"status":"completed"}}

Read this before adding a new slash command that coordinates multiple personas, or before introducing a new persona that \\\"wraps\\\" existing ones.\\n\\nThe governing rule: **the user (or a slash command) is the orchestrator. Personas do not invoke other personas.** Skills are mandatory hops inside a persona's workflow.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Endorsed patterns\\n\\n### 1. Direct invocation (no orchestration)\\n\\nSingle persona, single perspective, single artifact. The default and the cheapest option.\\n\\n```\\nuser → code-reviewer → report → user\\n```\\n\\n**Use when:** the work is one perspective on one artifact and you can describe it in one sentence.\\n\\n**Examples:**\\n- \\\"Review this PR\\\" → `code-reviewer`\\n- \\\"Find security issues in `auth.ts`\\\" → `security-auditor`\\n- \\\"What tests are missing for the checkout flow?\\\" → `test-engineer`\\n\\n**Cost:** one round trip. The baseline you should always compare orchestrated patterns against.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 2. Single-persona slash command\\n\\nA slash command that wraps one persona with the project's skills. Saves the user from re-explaining the workflow every time.\\n\\n```\\n/review → code-reviewer (with code-review-and-quality skill) → report\\n```\\n\\n**Use when:** the same single-persona invocation happens repeatedly with the same setup.\\n\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/review`, `/test`, `/code-simplify`.\\n\\n**Cost:** same as direct invocation. The slash command is just a saved prompt.\\n\\n**Anti-signal:** if the slash command's body is mostly \\\"decide which persona to call,\\\" delete it and let the user call the persona directly.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 3. Parallel fan-out with merge\\n\\nMultiple personas operate on the same input concurrently, each producing an independent report. A merge step (in the main agent's context) synthesizes them into a single decision.\\n\\n```\\n                    ┌─→ code-reviewer    ─┐\\n/ship → fan out  ───┼─→ security-auditor ─┤→ merge → go/no-go + rollback\\n                    └─→ test-engineer    ─┘\\n```\\n\\n**Use when:**\\n- The sub-tasks are genuinely independent (no shared mutable state, no ordering dependency)\\n- Each sub-agent benefits from its own context window\\n- The merge step is small enough to stay in the main context\\n- Wall-clock latency matters\\n\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/ship`.\\n\\n**Cost:** N parallel sub-agent contexts + one merge turn. Higher than direct invocation, but faster wall-clock and produces better reports because each sub-agent stays focused on its single perspective.\\n\\n**Validation checklist before adopting this pattern:**\\n- [ ] Can I run all sub-agents at the same time without ordering issues?\\n- [ ] Does each persona produce a different *kind* of finding, not just the same finding from a different angle?\\n- [ ] Will the merge step fit in the main agent's remaining context?\\n- [ ] Is the user's wait time long enough that parallelism is actually noticeable?\\n\\nIf any answer is \\\"no,\\\" fall back to direct invocation or a single-persona command.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 4. Sequential pipeline as user-driven slash commands\\n\\nThe user runs slash commands in a defined order, carrying context (or commit history) between them. There is no orchestrator agent — the user IS the orchestrator.\\n\\n```\\nuser runs:  /spec  →  /plan  →  /build  →  /test  →  /review  →  /ship\\n```\\n\\n**Use when:** the workflow has dependencies (each step needs the previous step's output) and human judgment between steps adds value.\\n\\n**Examples in this repo:** the entire DEFINE → PLAN → BUILD → VERIFY → REVIEW → SHIP lifecycle.\\n\\n**Cost:** one sub-agent context per step. Free for the orchestration layer because there is no orchestrator agent.\\n\\n**Why not automate it:** an LLM \\\"lifecycle orchestrator\\\" would (a) lose nuance between steps because it has to summarize for hand-off, (b) skip the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work early, and (c) double the token cost via paraphrasing turns.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 5. Research isolation (context preservation)\\n\\nWhen a task requires reading large amounts of material that shouldn't pollute the main context, spawn a research sub-agent that returns only a digest.\\n\\n```\\nmain agent → research sub-agent (reads 50 files) → digest → main agent continues\\n```\\n\\n**Use when:**\\n- The main session needs to stay focused on a downstream task\\n- The investigation result is much smaller than the input it consumes\\n- The decision quality benefits from the main agent having room to think after\\n\\n**Examples:** \\\"Find every call site of this deprecated API across the monorepo,\\\" \\\"Summarize what these 30 ADRs say about caching.\\\"\\n\\n**Cost:** one isolated sub-agent context. Worth it any time the alternative is loading hundreds of files into the main context.\\n\\n**On Claude Code, use the built-in `Explore` subagent** rather than defining a custom research persona. `Explore` runs on Haiku, is denied write/edit tools, and is purpose-built for this pattern. Define a custom research subagent only when `Explore` doesn't fit (e.g. you need a domain-specific system prompt the model wouldn't infer).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Claude Code compatibility\\n\\nThis catalog is harness-agnostic, but most readers will run it on Claude Code. Here's how each pattern maps onto Claude Code's primitives — and where the platform enforces our rules for us.\\n\\n### Where personas live\\n\\nPlugin subagents go in `agents/` at the plugin root. This repo is a plugin (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`), so `agents/code-reviewer.md`, `agents/security-auditor.md`, and `agents/test-engineer.md` are auto-discovered when the plugin is enabled. No path configuration needed.\\n\\n### Subagents vs. Agent Teams\\n\\nClaude Code has two parallelism primitives. Pattern 3 (parallel fan-out with merge) maps to **subagents**. If you need teammates that talk to each other, use **Agent Teams** instead.\\n\\n| | Subagents | Agent Teams |\\n|--|-----------|-------------|\\n| Coordination | Main agent fans out, sub-agents only report back | Teammates message each other, share a task list |\\n| Context | Own context window per subagent | Own context window per teammate |\\n| When to use | Independent tasks producing reports | Collaborative work needing discussion |\\n| Status | Stable | Experimental — requires `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` |\\n| Cost | Lower | Higher — each teammate is a separate Claude instance |\\n\\n**The personas in this repo work in both modes.** When spawned as subagents (e.g. by `/ship`), they report findings to the main session. When spawned as teammates (`Spawn a teammate using the security-auditor agent type…`), they can challenge each other's findings directly. The persona definition is the same; only the spawning context changes.\\n\\nOne subtlety: the `skills` and `mcpServers` frontmatter fields in a persona are honored when it runs as a subagent but **ignored when it runs as a teammate** — teammates load skills and MCP servers from your project and user settings, the same as a regular session. If a persona depends on a specific skill or MCP server being loaded, configure it at the session level so it's available in both modes.\\n\\n### Platform-enforced rules\\n\\nTwo rules in this catalog aren't just convention — Claude Code enforces them:\\n\\n- **\\\"Subagents cannot spawn other subagents\\\"** (verbatim from the docs). Anti-pattern B (persona-calls-persona) and Anti-pattern D (deep persona trees) cannot exist on Claude Code by construction.\\n- **\\\"No nested teams\\\"** — teammates cannot spawn their own teams. Same anti-patterns blocked at the team level.\\n\\nThis means you can adopt the patterns in this catalog without worrying about contributors accidentally building the anti-patterns. They'll just fail to load.\\n\\n### Built-in subagents to know about\\n\\nBefore defining a custom subagent, check whether one of these covers the role:\\n\\n| Built-in | Purpose |\\n|----------|---------|\\n| `Explore` | Read-only codebase search and analysis. Use this for Pattern 5 (research isolation). |\\n| `Plan` | Read-only research during plan mode. |\\n| `general-purpose` | Multi-step tasks needing both exploration and modification. |\\n\\nDon't redefine these. Layer your specialist personas (code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-engineer) on top of them.\\n\\n### Frontmatter restrictions for plugin agents\\n\\nPlugin subagents do **not** support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields — these are silently ignored. If a future persona needs any of those, the user must copy the file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` instead.\\n\\nThe fields that DO work in plugin agents are: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `memory`, `background`, `effort`, `isolation`, `color`, `initialPrompt`. Use `model` per-persona if you want to optimize cost (e.g. Haiku for `test-engineer` coverage scans, Sonnet for `code-reviewer`, Opus for `security-auditor`).\\n\\n### Spawning multiple subagents in parallel\\n\\nIn Claude Code, parallel fan-out (Pattern 3) requires issuing **multiple Agent tool calls in a single assistant turn**. Sequential turns serialize execution. `/ship` calls this out explicitly. Any new orchestrator command should do the same.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Worked example: Agent Teams for competing-hypothesis debugging\\n\\nThis example shows when to reach for **Agent Teams** instead of `/ship`'s subagent fan-out. The two patterns look similar from a distance — both spawn the same three personas — but the value comes from a different place.\\n\\n### The scenario\\n\\n> *Checkout occasionally hangs for ~30 seconds before completing. It happens roughly once every 50 sessions. No errors in logs. Started after last week's release.*\\n\\nPlausible root causes (mutually exclusive, all fit the symptoms):\\n\\n1. A race condition in the new payment-confirmation flow\\n2. An auth check that occasionally falls through to a slow synchronous network call\\n3. A missing index on a query that scales with cart size\\n4. A flaky third-party API where the SDK retries silently before timing out\\n\\nA single agent will pick the first plausible theory and stop investigating. A `/ship`-style subagent fan-out would have each persona report independently — but their reports never meet, so nothing rules out the wrong theories.\\n\\nThis is exactly the case the Agent Teams docs describe: *\\\"With multiple independent investigators actively trying to disprove each other, the theory that survives is much more likely to be the actual root cause.\\\"*\\n\\n### Why this is *not* a `/ship` job\\n\\n| | `/ship` (subagents) | Agent Teams |\\n|--|--------------------|-------------|\\n| Sub-agents see | The same diff, different lenses | A shared task list, each other's messages |\\n| Output | Three independent reports → one merge | Adversarial debate → consensus root cause |\\n| Right when | You want a verdict on a known artifact | You want to *find* the artifact among hypotheses |\\n\\n`/ship` is a verdict; Agent Teams is an investigation.\\n\\n### Setup (one-time, per-environment)\\n\\nAgent Teams is experimental. In `~/.claude/settings.json`:\\n\\n```json\\n{\\n  \\\"env\\\": {\\n    \\\"CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS\\\": \\\"1\\\"\\n  }\\n}\\n```\\n\\nRequires Claude Code v2.1.32 or later. The personas in this repo are picked up automatically — no team-config files to author by hand.\\n\\n### The trigger prompt\\n\\nType into the lead session, in natural language:\\n\\n```\\nUsers report checkout hangs for ~30 seconds intermittently after last\\nweek's release. No errors in logs.\\n\\nCreate an agent team to debug this with competing hypotheses. Spawn\\nthree teammates using the existing agent types:\\n\\n  - code-reviewer  — investigate race conditions and blocking calls\\n                     in the checkout code path\\n  - security-auditor — investigate auth checks, session handling,\\n                       and any synchronous network calls added recently\\n  - test-engineer  — propose tests that would distinguish between the\\n                     hypotheses and check coverage gaps in checkout\\n\\nHave them message each other directly to challenge each other's\\ntheories. Update findings as consensus emerges. Only converge when\\ntwo teammates agree they can disprove the others'.\\n```\\n\\nThe lead spawns three teammates referencing the existing persona names. The persona body is **appended** to each teammate's system prompt as additional instructions (on top of the team-coordination instructions the lead installs); the trigger prompt above becomes their task.\\n\\n### What happens\\n\\n1. Each teammate runs in its own context window, exploring the codebase from its own lens.\\n2. Teammates use `message` to send findings to each other directly. The lead doesn't have to relay.\\n3. The shared task list shows who's investigating what — visible at any time with `Ctrl+T` (in-process mode) or in a tmux pane (split mode).\\n4. When `code-reviewer` finds a `Promise.all` that should be sequential, it messages `security-auditor` to confirm the auth call isn't part of the race. `security-auditor` checks and replies — either confirming the race is the real issue or producing counter-evidence.\\n5. `test-engineer` proposes a focused integration test for whichever theory is winning, which the team uses to verify before declaring consensus.\\n6. The lead synthesizes the converged finding and presents it to you.\\n\\nYou can interrupt at any teammate by cycling with `Shift+Down` and typing — useful for redirecting an investigator who's gone down a wrong path.\\n\\n### When to clean up\\n\\nWhen the investigation lands on a root cause, tell the lead:\\n\\n```\\nClean up the team\\n```\\n\\nAlways cleanup through the lead, not a teammate (per the docs: teammates lack full team context for cleanup).\\n\\n### Cost expectation\\n\\nThree Sonnet teammates running for ~10–15 minutes of investigation costs noticeably more than the same three personas spawned as subagents by `/ship`. The justification is *quality of conclusion* — for production debugging where the wrong fix is expensive, the extra tokens are a bargain. For a routine PR review, stick with `/ship`.\\n\\n### Anti-pattern in this scenario\\n\\nDo **not** rebuild this as a `/debug` slash command that fans out subagents. Subagents can't message each other — you'd lose the adversarial debate that makes the pattern work. If a workflow keeps coming up, document the trigger prompt above as a snippet rather than wrapping it in a slash command that misuses subagents.\\n\\n### When *not* to use Agent Teams\\n\\n- Production-bound verdict on a known diff → use `/ship` (subagents).\\n- One specialist perspective on one artifact → direct persona invocation.\\n- Sequential lifecycle (spec → plan → build) → user-driven slash commands (Pattern 4).\\n- Read-heavy research with a small digest → built-in `Explore` subagent.\\n\\nReach for Agent Teams only when teammates **need** to challenge each other to produce the right answer.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Anti-patterns\\n\\n### A. Router persona (\\\"meta-orchestrator\\\")\\n\\nA persona whose job is to decide which other persona to call.\\n\\n```\\n/work → router-persona → \\\"this needs a review\\\" → code-reviewer → router (paraphrases) → user\\n```\\n\\n**Why it fails:**\\n- Pure routing layer with no domain value\\n- Adds two paraphrasing hops → information loss + roughly 2× token cost\\n- The user already knew they wanted a review; they could have called `/review` directly\\n- Replicates the work that slash commands and intent mapping in `AGENTS.md` already do\\n\\n**What to do instead:** add or refine slash commands. Document intent → command mapping in `AGENTS.md`.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### B. Persona that calls another persona\\n\\nA `code-reviewer` that internally invokes `security-auditor` when it sees auth code.\\n\\n**Why it fails:**\\n- Personas were designed to produce a single perspective; chaining them defeats that\\n- The summary the calling persona passes loses context the called persona needs\\n- Failure modes multiply (which persona's output format wins? whose rules apply?)\\n- Hides cost from the user\\n\\n**What to do instead:** have the calling persona *recommend* a follow-up audit in its report. The user or a slash command runs the second pass.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### C. Sequential orchestrator that paraphrases\\n\\nAn agent that calls `/spec`, then `/plan`, then `/build`, etc. on the user's behalf.\\n\\n**Why it fails:**\\n- Loses the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work\\n- Each hand-off summarizes context — accumulated drift over a long pipeline\\n- Doubles token cost: orchestrator turn + sub-agent turn for every step\\n- Removes user agency at exactly the points where judgment matters most\\n\\n**What to do instead:** keep the user as the orchestrator. Document the recommended sequence in `README.md` and let users invoke it.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### D. Deep persona trees\\n\\n`/ship` calls a `pre-ship-coordinator` that calls a `quality-coordinator` that calls `code-reviewer`.\\n\\n**Why it fails:**\\n- Each layer adds latency and tokens with no decision value\\n- Debugging becomes a multi-level investigation\\n- The leaf personas lose context to multiple summarization steps\\n\\n**What to do instead:** keep the orchestration depth at most 1 (slash command → personas). The merge happens in the main agent.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Decision flow\\n\\nWhen considering a new orchestrated workflow, walk this flow:\\n\\n```\\nIs the work one perspective on one artifact?\\n├── Yes → Direct invocation. Stop.\\n└── No  → Will the same composition repeat?\\n         ├── No  → Direct invocation, ad hoc. Stop.\\n         └── Yes → Are sub-tasks independent?\\n                  ├── No  → Sequential slash commands run by user (Pattern 4).\\n                  └── Yes → Parallel fan-out with merge (Pattern 3).\\n                           Validate against the checklist above.\\n                           If any check fails → fall back to single-persona command (Pattern 2).\\n```\\n\\n---\\n\\n## When to add a new pattern to this catalog\\n\\nAdd a new entry only after:\\n\\n1. You've used the pattern at least twice in real work\\n2. You can name a concrete artifact in this repo that demonstrates it\\n3. You can explain why an existing pattern wouldn't have worked\\n4. You can describe its anti-pattern shadow (what people will mistakenly build instead)\\n\\nPremature catalog entries become aspirational documentation that no one follows.\\n\",\n  \"encoding\": \"base64\",\n  \"_links\": {\n    \"self\": \"https://api.github.com/repos/addyosmani/agent-skills/contents/references/orchestration-patterns.md?ref=main\",\n    \"git\": \"https://api.github.com/repos/addyosmani/agent-skills/git/blobs/09cddd31d52a95be1d9bca814547d184b9945e44\",\n    \"html\": \"https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/blob/main/references/orchestration-patterns.md\"\n  }\n}"}],"structured_content":null},"error":null,"status":"completed"}}

Discovery/routing drift: both legacy `ce-*` and target `he-*` identifiers could exist in different layers, making stage selection and references inconsistent.\\n2. Validation-gate breakage: the skill-authoring family gate still referenced CE-era variables and path precedence, which caused pre-commit failures during the cutover.\\n\\nThis made the migration non-durable until naming, routing, and validation enforcement all converged on HE canonical names.\\n\\n## Resolution\\n\\nApplied a complete cutover with canonical HE naming plus validator hardening:\\n\\n1. Renamed active harness-engineering skills from `ce-*` to `he-*` and updated plugin/routing metadata to HE identifiers.\\n2. Normalized preserved skill fixtures (then `Plugins/harness-engineering/fixtures/skill-archive`, now `Plugins/harness-engineering/fixtures/preserved-context` with a compatibility alias) from `ce-*` to `he-*`, including anti-pattern reference filenames and task-profile IDs.\\n3. Updated `Infrastructure/scripts/validation-and-linting/validate_skill_authoring_family.sh` to:\\n   - validate `he-work`/`he-tdd` approval-flow linkage,\\n   - fix stale CE variable references,\\n   - prefer canonical `Plugins/...` pytest candidates before lowercase fallback aliases.\\n4. Re-ran family-gate and hook paths until commit/push hooks passed with the migrated naming model.\\n\\nResult: HE naming is now the active canonical path in skills, archive fixtures, routing, and pre-commit enforcement.\\n\\n## Evidence\\n\\n- Commit and scope:\\n  - `b7cfa722` (`refactor(harness-engineering): complete ce-to-he skill cutover`)\\n  - 217 files changed with active + archive rename coverage and validator updates.\\n- Validation command:\\n  - `bash Infrastructure/scripts/validation-and-linting/validate_skill_authoring_family.sh` -> pass\\n  - includes pytest lane: `24 passed`.\\n- Hook outcomes:\\n  - commit hook `Run pre-commit validation` -> pass\\n  - push hook `Run pre-push diagnostics` -> pass\\n- Branch and PR:\\n  - branch: `codex/agent-skills-worktree-c81e0239`\\n  - PR: `https://github.com/jscraik/Agent-Skills/pull/127`\\n\\n## Follow-up\\n\\n- Keep HE-only names as canonical in plugin manifests, routing maps, and stage docs; treat new CE-name reintroduction as drift.\\n- Require independent CodeRabbit/Codex review artifacts on PR #127 before merge, since this migration changes broad path and routing surfaces.\\n- If any external consumers still reference `ce-*`, capture those callers explicitly and either migrate them or add bounded compatibility shims with sunset dates.\\n\", \"encoding\": \"utf-8\", \"sha\": \"45ae5cb01faa05d93326ef9fea1e94f61db2478f\", \"display_url\": \"https://github.com/jscraik/Agent-Skills/blob/98fee9a7855596e6861e3a0ed71a76bb3995bffa/Docs/solutions/2026-04-20-harness-engineering-ce-to-he-migration-cutover.md\", \"display_title\": \"2026-04-20-harness-engineering-ce-to-he-migration-cutover.md\"}"}],"structured_content":null},"error":null,"status":"completed"}}

The repository already has strong skill metadata and governance mechanisms, but lacks a dedicated routing layer for first-choice quality.\\n\\nPrimary motivation carried forward from brainstorm: improve **first-hit routing accuracy** while preserving deterministic behavior and governance controls (see brainstorm: `docs/brainstorms/2026-03-04-skill-router-brainstorm.md`).\\n\\n## Research Summary\\n### Brainstorm origin (primary input)\\n- Chosen approach: deterministic scorecard router.\\n- Rejected alternatives (for v1):\\n  - deterministic + confirm-step as default,\\n  - hybrid rules+LLM tie-break.\\n- Scope constraints:\\n  - top-3 + confidence + rationale output contract,\\n  - optimize for both humans and agents,\\n  - CLI/report-first delivery.\\n\\n(All above carried forward from: `docs/brainstorms/2026-03-04-skill-router-brainstorm.md`.)\\n\\n### Local repo findings\\n- Skill system is canonicalized around `SKILL.md` plus flat symlink sync flow (`README.md:176-180`, `Infrastructure/scripts/lifecycle-and-sync/sync_skills.sh:126`, `Infrastructure/scripts/lifecycle-and-sync/sync_skills.sh:158`).\\n- Existing recursive loop explicitly models routing concepts and router execution mode (`docs/skill-graphs/index.md:10`).\\n- Genome loop already computes routing confusion and candidate confidence controls (`Infrastructure/scripts/lifecycle-and-sync/run_skill_genome_loop.py:241`, `Infrastructure/scripts/lifecycle-and-sync/run_skill_genome_loop.py:391`, `Infrastructure/scripts/lifecycle-and-sync/run_skill_genome_loop.py:37-39`).\\n- Existing runbook defines candidate fields and fail-closed redaction posture (`docs/skill-graphs/runbooks/skill-genome-loop.md:92-115`, `docs/skill-graphs/runbooks/skill-genome-loop.md:147`).\\n- AGENTS requirements emphasize explicit tooling, discovery order, and docs TOC (`AGENTS.md:74`, `AGENTS.md:101`, `AGENTS.md:14`).\\n\\n### Institutional learnings (closest equivalent)\\n- No `docs/solutions/` entries were found for this topic.\\n- Closest internal equivalents:\\n  - `docs/brainstorms/2026-02-24-skill-graph-live-auto-learning-brainstorm.md`\\n  - `Docs/plans/2026-02-24-feat-skill-graph-live-auto-learning-plan.md`\\n  - `docs/skill-graphs/runbooks/skill-genome-loop.md`\\n  - `docs/skill-graphs/knowledge-graph-operating-model.md`\\n\\n### External research decision\\nNo external research performed. Reason: low external-risk domain, strong internal patterns already present, and clear origin decisions from the brainstorm.\\n\\n### SpecFlow analysis highlights incorporated\\n- Define deterministic tie-break contract.\\n- Define confidence bands and machine-readable schema.\\n- Define low/zero-confidence fallback behavior.\\n- Define actor-specific first-hit instrumentation.\\n- Define non-interactive execution policy for agents.\\n- Add adversarial/abuse fixtures and telemetry redaction invariants.\\n\\n## Proposed Solution\\nCreate a scorecard-based router layer that evaluates each skill candidate using deterministic rules and outputs ranked top-3 recommendations.\\n\\n### Core v1 behavior\\n1. Normalize input request.\\n2. Load active skill catalog from canonical source.\\n3. Apply deterministic feature scoring (trigger overlap, explicit mention, anti-trigger penalties, context alignment).\\n4. Stable sort with deterministic tie-breakers.\\n5. Return top-3 with confidence + rationale in both human and JSON views.\\n6. Emit routing telemetry for first-hit KPI tracking.\\n\\n### Why this approach\\nThis is the smallest useful slice that preserves auditability and governance while improving routing quality (see brainstorm: `docs/brainstorms/2026-03-04-skill-router-brainstorm.md`). It avoids premature model dependency and keeps failure modes explicit.\\n\\n## Alternative Approaches Considered\\n1. **Deterministic + mandatory confirm step**\\n   - Benefit: lower accidental auto-selection risk.\\n   - Rejection for v1: adds interaction overhead before baseline signal is established (see brainstorm: `docs/brainstorms/2026-03-04-skill-router-brainstorm.md`).\\n2. **Hybrid rules + LLM tie-breaker**\\n   - Benefit: potentially stronger handling for highly ambiguous requests.\\n   - Rejection for v1: increased complexity, lower auditability, and harder deterministic testing (see brainstorm: `docs/brainstorms/2026-03-04-skill-router-brainstorm.md`).\\n\\n## Premortem (Failure Scenario: 2026-09-04)\\nSix months later, the router rollout is considered a failure. First-hit accuracy improved on paper but trust declined. Users bypassed suggestions, agents misrouted high-confidence tasks, and maintainers disabled active mode.\\n\\n### What went wrong\\n- Confidence scores were overfit and poorly calibrated; \\u201chigh confidence\\u201d often meant \\u201cmost keyword overlap,\\u201d not true intent.\\n- Skill catalog drifted (stale sync, inconsistent metadata quality), so deterministic ranking was deterministically wrong.\\n- Ambiguous and multi-intent prompts were forced into single-intent ranking without strong uncertainty handling.\\n- Human and agent execution policies diverged in practice; agent consumers auto-ran risky suggestions.\\n- Metrics were gameable (top-1 acceptance rose because UI nudged top candidate).\\n- Telemetry quality was noisy/incomplete, reducing ability to detect regressions early.\\n\\n### False assumptions\\n- Assumed skill descriptions/triggers were sufficiently clean for reliable scoring.\\n- Assumed deterministic output alone would create user trust.\\n- Assumed low-confidence fallback states were rare.\\n- Assumed one KPI (first-hit) captured real quality and user value.\\n\\n### Edge cases missed\\n- Negation prompts (\\u201cdon\\u2019t use X\\u201d), mixed intents, and comparative asks.\\n- Typos, alias drift, deprecated skills, and synonym gaps.\\n- Long prompts with conflicting cues and non-English phrasing.\\n- Requests mentioning dangerous capabilities where auto-run should never trigger.\\n\\n### Integration issues overlooked\\n- Catalog version mismatch between router and consumer runtimes.\\n- Incomplete contract tests across CLI, JSON consumers, and agent orchestration.\\n- Missing strong gates for rollout-state propagation and rollback drills.\\n\\n### What users hated\\n- Opaque rationales (\\u201cmatched keywords\\u201d) that felt generic.\\n- Confidently wrong top suggestion appearing repeatedly.\\n- Too much friction on uncertain prompts and too little safety on risky ones.\\n\\n## Plan Revisions from Premortem\\nTo reduce these failure modes, this plan now adds:\\n1. **Calibration-first rollout:** mandatory baseline dataset + calibration checks before active mode.\\n2. **Quality-gated metadata:** catalog freshness and SKILL metadata quality checks as preconditions.\\n3. **Uncertainty and safety-first policy:** explicit no-auto-run rules for risky/ambiguous cases.\\n4. **Anti-gaming metrics:** add override regret and correction-latency metrics, not just top-1 acceptance.\\n5. **Cross-surface contract testing:** strict roundtrip tests for CLI, JSON, and agent consumers.\\n6. **Operational resilience:** hard control precedence, rollback drills, and auto-downgrade triggers.\\n\\n## Technical Considerations\\n- **Architecture impacts**\\n  - Introduce a routing contract layer separate from existing skill definitions.\\n  - Reuse current metadata pipeline (`SKILL.md` index and sync artifacts) rather than adding a second skill registry.\\n  - Keep rollout controls compatible with existing `off | observe_only | active` posture.\\n\\n- **Performance implications**\\n  - Target low-latency local ranking for interactive CLI usage.\\n  - Use precomputed skill metadata snapshot where possible.\\n  - Keep deterministic sort and scoring O(n) or O(n log n) over skill count.\\n\\n- **Security considerations**\\n  - Do not persist raw sensitive prompt text in routing logs.\\n  - Enforce telemetry allowlist + redaction-at-write.\\n  - Ensure non-interactive mode cannot silently auto-run low-confidence routes.\\n  - Default `agent_mode=observe_only` until rollout gates pass.\\n\\n## System-Wide Impact\\n- **Interaction graph**\\n  - Request ingestion triggers router scoring, which produces ranked candidates, then selected skill execution, then telemetry logging.\\n  - In observe-only mode, execution behavior remains unchanged; only recommendation + telemetry layers are added.\\n\\n- **Error propagation**\\n  - Catalog load or schema errors must return machine-readable error payloads and non-zero exit.\\n  - Low-confidence is not an error; it is an explicit routing state with fallback guidance.\\n  - Invalid controls (missing/unreadable/malformed) fail closed to safe mode (`observe_only` or `off`).\\n\\n- **State lifecycle risks**\\n  - Risk: stale skill index causing poor recommendations.\\n  - Mitigation: include Infrastructure/catalog/version metadata in each router result and block active mode when freshness checks fail.\\n\\n- **API surface parity**\\n  - Human CLI report and JSON output must reflect identical ranking and confidence values.\\n  - Agent consumers must rely on the same schema version used by CLI JSON output.\\n\\n- **Integration test scenarios**\\n  1. Ambiguous request with two near-equal candidates yields stable order across repeated runs.\\n  2. Explicit skill mention always outranks generic intent-only matches.\\n  3. Non-interactive low-confidence request returns `requires_clarification=true` and no implicit auto-run.\\n  4. Broken skill metadata entry is skipped/flagged without crashing full ranking.\\n  5. First-hit telemetry records rank-chosen and actor type correctly.\\n  6. Multi-intent and negation prompts produce uncertainty flags instead of false-confidence routing.\\n\\n## Implementation Phases\\n### Phase 1: Contract + control foundation\\n- Define invocation boundary contract (input shape, actor type, policy mode, output/error contract).\\n- Define router output schema v1 (human + JSON parity).\\n- Define telemetry allowlist/redaction contract with forbidden fields.\\n- Define deterministic scoring/tie-break specification and confidence bands.\\n- Define rollout control precedence (`kill-switch > rollback-required > rollout-mode`) with fail-closed behavior.\\n\\n### Phase 2: Data quality + calibration foundation\\n- Build benchmark fixture set (clear, ambiguous, adversarial, multi-intent, negation, deprecated aliases).\\n- Define calibration policy (threshold bands + acceptable error rates by actor type).\\n- Add catalog freshness/version checks tied to sync pipeline.\\n- Add metadata quality checks (required fields, trigger completeness, anti-trigger presence where applicable).\\n\\n### Phase 3: Router execution path\\n- Implement input normalization and candidate scoring.\\n- Implement deterministic ranking and rationale generation.\\n- Add CLI/report rendering and JSON output mode.\\n- Add explicit uncertainty handling for ambiguous/multi-intent prompts.\\n\\n### Phase 4: Metrics + controlled rollout\\n- Add first-hit instrumentation by actor type (`human|agent`).\\n- Add anti-gaming metrics (override regret, correction latency, repeat-misroute rate).\\n- Add observe-only rollout baseline window and go/no-go thresholds.\\n- Add rollback drill and kill-switch propagation verification before active mode.\\n- Add auto-downgrade triggers back to `observe_only` on safety/quality regressions.\\n\\n## name: toml
description: Create and review TOML configuration with strict typing and predictable structure. Use when editing tool configuration files that require schema-safe TOML.
metadata:
  skill-type: code_quality_review
---

## Table of Contents

- [When to use](#when-to-use)
- [Required inputs](#required-inputs)
- [Deliverables](#deliverables)
- [Philosophy](#philosophy)
- [Procedure](#procedure)
- [TOML Guidelines](#toml-guidelines)
- [Editing Rules](#editing-rules)
- [Validation](#validation)
- [Constraints](#constraints)
- [Anti-patterns](#anti-patterns)
- [Failure mode](#failure-mode)
- [Gotchas](#gotchas)
- [References](#references)

## When to use

- Use for TOML config creation, review, or schema-safe fixes.
- Inputs: target files, owning tool, expected key paths, and compatibility constraints.
- Deliver valid TOML with minimal key-path churn and notes for schema-impacting edits.

## Required inputs

- Target TOML file path and owning tool or schema.
- Intended key paths, value types, and compatibility constraints.
- Validation command or parser expected to consume the file.

## Deliverables

- Minimal TOML edit preserving existing comments and order where possible.
- Validation evidence from parser, schema, or owning tool.
- Notes for any type, key-path, or compatibility risk.

## Philosophy

- Prefer schema truth and low-churn edits over clever rewrites.

## Procedure

1. Confirm the consumer schema and current key paths.
2. Make the smallest compatible edit.
3. Validate before closeout.

## TOML Guidelines

- Preserve key order where tool owners expect readability.
- Prefer explicit scalars and arrays over ambiguous shapes.
- Keep one responsibility per table and use dotted keys consistently.
- Do not mix inline tables and expanded tables for the same object path.

## Editing Rules

- Change only the smallest required key path.
- Retain existing comments unless provably outdated.
- Keep trailing commas out of arrays and inline tables.

## Validation

- Run the relevant parser/schema/tool checks for touched files.
- Fail fast: stop at the first failed gate and report exact blocker evidence.

## Constraints

- If schema ownership is unclear, pause before adding keys.
- Redact secrets and do not run destructive or network commands unless explicitly approved.

## Anti-patterns

- Redefining key paths, mixing table styles for one object, or skipping validation.

## Failure mode

If the owning schema, value type, or validation command cannot be identified, stop and report the missing contract before editing.

## Gotchas

- Quoting numeric values can silently change type semantics.

## See Also

|---|---|
| [[yaml]] | Schema-aware config review for YAML-based tooling configs |
| [[he-fix-bugs]] | Triage config parsing failures with evidence-first diagnosis |

set -euo pipefail

changed_files=()
changed_files_mode=0

while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
  case "$1" in
    --changed-files)
      changed_files_mode=1
      shift
      while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
        if [[ "$1" == --* ]]; then
          break
        fi
        changed_files+=("${1#./}")
        shift
      done
      continue

    --help|-h)

Usage: bash Infrastructure/scripts/validation-and-linting/validate_skill_authoring_family.sh [--changed-files <file>...]

EOF

      ;;
    *)

      exit 2
      ;;
  esac
  shift
done

# changed_files_match returns success when any provided changed file matches the supplied glob.
changed_files_match() {
  local pattern="$1"
  local changed_file=""
  for changed_file in "${changed_files[@]}"; do
    # shellcheck disable=SC2053
    if [[ "$changed_file" == $pattern ]]; then

  return 1

def _write_manifest(root: Path, skill_set: str, rows: list[dict[str, object]]) -> None:
    manifest_dir = root / skill_set
    manifest_dir.mkdir(parents=True)
    with (manifest_dir / "manifest.jsonl").open("w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for row in rows:
            handle.write(json.dumps(row) + "\n")


def _write_source_files(root: Path, rows: list[dict[str, object]]) -> None:
    for row in rows:

        if not source_path or "Plugins/missing/" in source_path:

        skill_file = root / source_path
        skill_file.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        skill_file.write_text("# Test skill\n", encoding="utf-8")

## Hybrid Threshold Policy

These thresholds must be satisfied for any release-grade readiness claim. They are enforced during the P3 gate check and ongoing quality monitoring.

### Absolute Floors

| Skill | Dimension | Floor |
|---|---|---|
| `skill-installer` | Variation | ≥ 8/15 |
| `skill-installer` | Empowerment | ≥ 3/5 |
| `skill-installer` | Scope Focus | ≥ 12/15 |
| `plugin-creator` | Variation | ≥ 8/15 |
| `plugin-creator` | Empowerment | ≥ 3/5 |
| `plugin-creator` | Scope Focus | ≥ 12/15 |

### Required Uplift Delta from Pre-Uplift Baseline

| Skill | Dimension | Required Delta |
|---|---|---|
| `skill-installer` | Variation | ≥ +2 (achieved: +10) |
| `skill-installer` | Empowerment | ≥ +1 (achieved: +5) |

| `plugin-creator` | Scope Focus | ≥ +1 (achieved: +9) |

All required uplift deltas were exceeded in the P3 pass.

## No-Regression Guardrails

These rules apply to any future SKILL.md changes for `skill-installer` and `plugin-creator`:

1. **Overall analyzer score must not decrease** from the post-uplift baseline.
2. **No individual dimension score may decrease by more than 1 point** from post-uplift values without an explicit change note in this document.
3. **No role-overlap regressions**: routing language must not re-introduce cross-family confusion or scope ambiguity.
4. **Scope focus for plugin-creator**: the improvement achieved by reducing surface mentions (from 6 to ≤3 surface patterns in body text) must be preserved. If future edits re-introduce `\bhooks?\b`, `\bapps?\b`, or `\bmcp\b` references in prose, scope focus will regress. Use generic descriptions (e.g., "companion folder flags") when discussing optional scaffold types.

  "content": "# Ubiquitous Language\n\n## Scope and Sources\n\n- Scope: `agent-skills` repository operations, skill authoring, skill sync, and runtime visibility.\n- Sources: current conversation, `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `Docs/agents/14-path-ownership-boundaries.md`, `Docs/agents/13-workflow-and-safety-guidance.md`, `Infrastructure/scripts/lifecycle-and-sync/selection_policy.py`, and `Skills/agent-ops/ubiquitous-language/SKILL.md`.\n- Last updated: 2026-04-26\n\n## Canonical Terms\n\n| Term | Definition | Aliases to avoid | Confidence |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| **Agent Skills Kit** | The governed repository and CLI system for authoring, validating, discovering, and syncing Codex skills. | skills repo, agent-skills stuff | High |\n| **`ask` CLI** | The public command interface at `./bin/ask` that agents must use for repository operations. | helper script, ask wrapper | High |\n| **Canonical Skill Source** | The editable source of a skill under `Skills/<topic-cluster>/<skill-name>/` or a plugin-owned skill path. | runtime skill, synced copy | High |\n| **Runtime Projection** | The generated skill view under `.agents/skills/**` that Codex and agent runtimes consume. | canonical skill, source skill | High |\n| **Generated Command Handle** | A small generated `SKILL.md` under `.agents/skills/<handle>/` that makes `$<handle>` mentionable and may include a `source_path` that resolves to a canonical skill source (generated by `Infrastructure/scripts/lifecycle-and-sync/command_surface.py`), or may be absent/unresolved (i.e., a pointer/stub only). It is a pointer, not the real workflow. The `source_path` is optional and may be missing or unresolved. | command stub, runtime stub, copied skill | High |\n| **User Runtime Links** | The home-directory links `~/.agents/skills` and `Plugins/<plugin>`, run the relevant plugin validation, then run `./bin/ask skills sync --scope user --projection rooted` or `./bin/ask plugins sync-local-runtime` so copied plugin mirrors are replaced.\" |\n\n## Relationships\n\n- A **Canonical Skill Source** may produce one **Runtime Projection** entry after **Workspace Sync**.\n- A **Runtime Projection** entry becomes available to user-level Codex sessions through **User Runtime Links** after **User Sync**.\n- A **Generated Command Handle** exists only to make a routed skill mentionable, for example `$he-heartbeat`; the real Recommendation: name the absolute path when reporting where commands ran.\n- \"Make it visible\" can mean adding files to source control or adding a skill to **Visible Runtime Surface**. Recommendation: say **Generated Command Handle** for `$`-mentionable runtime pointers and reserve \"stub\" for test doubles or temporary executable placeholders.\n\n## Agent Integration\n\n- Instruction surface updated: `AGENTS.md`\n- Integration summary: future agents are told to read this glossary before changing skills, sync policy, runtime projections, or agent-facing docs, and to use Prompt Translations for terse or ambiguous user phrases.\n- Validation/enforcement: manual glossary validation in this run; no new validator added yet.\n\n## Decisions\n\n- `ubiquitous-language` is intentionally included in `DEFAULT_VISIBLE_FLAT_SKILL_NAMES` because it governs how terse user language maps to repo-native agent actions; revisit only if default skill-context pressure becomes a measured problem.\n\n## Open Questions\n\n- Should this glossary become a maintained repository contract linked from `AGENTS.md`, or remain an operator aid until the vocabulary stabilizes?\n- Should the repo add a dedicated validation check that flags a canonical skill copied into `Skills/**` but absent from both the visible runtime surface and documented advanced discovery paths?\n",

  "content": "# Ubiquitous Language\n\n## Scope and Sources\n\n- Scope: `agent-skills` repository operations, skill authoring, skill sync, and runtime visibility.\n- Sources: current conversation, `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `Docs/agents/14-path-ownership-boundaries.md`, `Docs/agents/13-workflow-and-safety-guidance.md`, `Infrastructure/scripts/lifecycle-and-sync/selection_policy.py`, and `Skills/agent-ops/ubiquitous-language/SKILL.md`.\n- Last updated: 2026-04-26\n\n## Canonical Terms\n\n| Term | Definition | Aliases to avoid | Confidence |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| **Agent Skills Kit** | The governed repository and CLI system for authoring, validating, discovering, and syncing Codex skills. | skills repo, agent-skills stuff | High |\n| **`ask` CLI** | The public command interface at `./bin/ask` that agents must use for repository operations. | helper script, ask wrapper | High |\n| **Canonical Skill Source** | The editable source of a skill under `Skills/<topic-cluster>/<skill-name>/` or a plugin-owned skill path. | runtime skill, synced copy | High |\n| **Runtime Projection** | The generated skill view under `.agents/skills/**` that Codex and agent runtimes consume. | canonical skill, source skill | High |\n| **Generated Command Handle** | A small generated `SKILL.md` under `.agents/skills/<handle>/` that makes `$<handle>` mentionable and may include a `source_path` that resolves to a canonical skill source (generated by `Infrastructure/scripts/lifecycle-and-sync/command_surface.py`), or may be absent/unresolved (i.e., a pointer/stub only). It is a pointer, not the real workflow. The `source_path` is optional and may be missing or unresolved. | command stub, runtime stub, copied skill | High |\n| **User Runtime Links** | The home-directory links `~/.agents/skills` and `~/.codex/skills` that point to the active runtime projection. | user sync, installed skills | High |\n| **Plugin Runtime Mirror** | A real copied plugin tree, such as `~/plugins` or a Codex profile `Plugins/`, refreshed from canonical `~/dev/agent-skills/Plugins` so marketplace paths resolve without aliasing repo source. | plugin symlink, canonical plugin root | High |\n| **Workspace Sync** | The operation `./bin/ask skills sync --scope workspace` that refreshes repo-local runtime projections and the generated root `SKILL.md` index. | sync the repo, update links | High |\n| **User Sync** | The operation `./bin/ask skills sync --scope user` that points user-level runtime skill directories at the current workspace projection. | install skills, make Codex see it | High |\n| **Visible Runtime Surface** | The bounded default skill list exposed by `DEFAULT_VISIBLE_FLAT_SKILL_NAMES` to control always-loaded skill context. | skill list, visible skills | High |\n| **Advanced Repo Discovery** | Repository scan mode that can find skills not promoted into the default visible runtime surface. | hidden skill, missing skill | Medium |\n| **Feature Worktree** | A separate checkout and branch used for isolated feature work without disturbing dirty changes in the primary checkout. | worktree, clean checkout | High |\n| **Projection Refresh Lane** | A bounded change path where generated projections are refreshed from canonical sources instead of hand-edited. | sync pass, generated update | Medium |\n| **Strict Skill Audit** | The `./bin/ask skills audit <path> --level strict` check that validates skill structure, runtime links, security gates, family benchmarks, and readiness. | check the skill, make sure it works | High |\n| **Mise Trust Blocker** | A local runtime state where `mise` refuses to load the worktree config until the specific `.mise.toml` is trusted. | mise broken, toolchain issue | High |\n| **Policy Identity** | The deterministic hash representing the active selection and discovery policy. | policy hash, sync hash | Medium |\n\n## Prompt Translations\n\n| User phrase | Canonical intent | Better Codex wording |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| \"sync my skills\" | Refresh the active workspace projection and point user runtime links at it. | \"Run `./bin/ask skills sync --scope workspace --json`, then `./bin/ask skills sync --scope user --json`, and verify `~/.codex/skills` points at this worktree.\" |\n| \"find the ubiquitous-language skill\" | Locate the canonical skill source and determine whether the runtime projection exposes it. | \"Search `Skills/**`, `Plugins/**`, `.agents/skills/**`, and `./bin/ask skills list --json` for `ubiquitous-language`, then report source path and runtime visibility separately.\" |\n| \"so you will not be able to use it?\" | Distinguish manual filesystem access from formal runtime skill availability. | \"Check whether the skill is available through the active `~/.codex/skills` projection; if not, state whether it can still be read manually from disk.\" |\n| \"proceed\" | Carry out the previously described corrective path. | \"Copy the missing canonical skill into this feature worktree, promote it to the visible runtime surface if needed, sync workspace and user scopes, then validate discoverability.\" |\n| \"run the skill\" | Execute the skill workflow in the current repo scope and produce its expected artifact. | \"Use `$ubiquitous-language` to create or update repo-root `UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md`, citing source files and validating the output file exists.\" |\n| \"make it available\" | Ensure Codex runtime discovery can see a skill, not just that source files exist. | \"Add the skill to the default visible runtime surface when appropriate, run workspace and user sync, and verify `./bin/ask skills list --json` includes it.\" |\n| \"check it works\" | Produce fresh evidence for the changed surface. | \"Run the smallest relevant validation command for the changed skill or sync policy and report exact pass/fail/blocker output.\" |\n| \"update the plugin\" | Change the canonical plugin source and refresh materialized runtime mirrors. | \"Patch `Plugins/<plugin>`, run the relevant plugin validation, then run `./bin/ask skills sync --scope user --projection rooted` or `./bin/ask plugins sync-local-runtime` so copied plugin mirrors are replaced.\" |\n\n## Relationships\n\n- A **Canonical Skill Source** may produce one **Runtime Projection** entry after **Workspace Sync**.\n- A **Runtime Projection** entry becomes available to user-level Codex sessions through **User Runtime Links** after **User Sync**.\n- A **Generated Command Handle** exists only to make a routed skill mentionable, for example `$he-heartbeat`; the real workflow remains in the resolved **Canonical Skill Source**. If `./bin/ask` is unavailable outside this repository, load the handle's embedded `source_path` directly before falling back to owner-tree search.\n- `~/.agents/plugins` is a live symlink to canonical `Plugins/`, while **Plugin Runtime Mirrors** such as `~/plugins` are real copied directories and must be refreshed after plugin source or marketplace changes.\n- A skill can exist in **Advanced Repo Discovery** while remaining absent from the **Visible Runtime Surface**.\n- The **Visible Runtime Surface** is controlled by `DEFAULT_VISIBLE_FLAT_SKILL_NAMES`, not by the mere presence of a `SKILL.md` file.\n- A **Feature Worktree** can intentionally diverge from the primary checkout; uncommitted skills in the primary checkout are not automatically present in the feature worktree.\n- **Strict Skill Audit** depends on local runtime health; a **Mise Trust Blocker** must be fixed before treating audit failure as a skill defect.\n- `SKILL.md` at the repo root is a generated index surface and should be refreshed by sync, not hand-edited.\n\n## Example Dialogue\n\n> **Dev:** \"When I say `sync my skills`, do I mean just update `SKILL.md`?\"\n>\n> **Domain expert:** \"No. In this repo, translate that into workspace sync plus user sync, then verify the home-directory runtime links.\"\n>\n> **Dev:** \"If a skill is on disk, is Codex able to use it?\"\n>\n> **Domain expert:** \"Only if the active runtime projection exposes it. Source existence and runtime visibility are related but not the same.\"\n>\n> **Dev:** \"Why did `ubiquitous-language` not appear after copying it?\"\n>\n> **Domain expert:** \"Because it existed in the canonical source tree but was not yet part of the visible runtime surface. Recommendation: use **Canonical Skill Source** for editable files, **Runtime Projection** for `.agents/skills/**`, and **available skill** for what the active Codex session can invoke.\n- \"Sync\" can mean **Workspace Sync**, **User Sync**, or a lower-level projection refresh script. Recommendation: default to both `./bin/ask skills sync --scope workspace` and `./bin/ask skills sync --scope user` when the user says \"sync my skills.\"\n- \"Use it\" can mean manually reading a skill's instructions or invoking it through runtime skill discovery. Recommendation: answer both availability paths when a skill was just added.\n- \"Worktree\" can mean the original dirty checkout or the new feature checkout. Recommendation: name the absolute path when reporting where commands ran.\n- \"Make it visible\" can mean adding files to source control or adding a skill to **Visible Runtime Surface**. Recommendation: verify with `./bin/ask skills list --json`, not only `find`.\n- \"Stub\" is overloaded. Recommendation: say **Generated Command Handle** for `$`-mentionable runtime pointers and reserve \"stub\" for test doubles or temporary executable placeholders.\n\n## Agent Integration\n\n- Instruction surface updated: `AGENTS.md`\n- Integration summary: future agents are told to read this glossary before changing skills, sync policy, runtime projections, or agent-facing docs, and to use Prompt Translations for terse or ambiguous user phrases.\n- Validation/enforcement: manual glossary validation in this run; no new validator added yet.\n\n## Decisions\n\n- `ubiquitous-language` is intentionally included in `DEFAULT_VISIBLE_FLAT_SKILL_NAMES` because it governs how terse user language maps to repo-native agent actions; revisit only if default skill-context pressure becomes a measured problem.\n\n## Open Questions\n\n- Should this glossary become a maintained repository contract linked from `AGENTS.md`, or remain an operator aid until the vocabulary stabilizes?\n- Should the repo add a dedicated validation check that flags a canonical skill copied into `Skills/**` but absent from both the visible runtime surface and documented advanced discovery paths?\n",

  "content": "# Agent Personas\n\nSpecialist personas that play a single role with a single perspective. Each persona is a Markdown file consumed as a system prompt by your harness (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, etc.).\n\n| Persona | Role | Best for |\n|---------|------|----------|\n| [code-reviewer](code-reviewer.md) | Senior Staff Engineer | Five-axis review before merge |\n| [security-auditor](security-auditor.md) | Security Engineer | Vulnerability detection, OWASP-style audit |\n| [test-engineer](test-engineer.md) | QA Engineer | Test strategy, coverage analysis, Prove-It pattern |\n\n## How personas relate to skills and commands\n\nThree layers, each with a distinct job:\n\n| Layer | What it is | Example | Composition role |\n|-------|-----------|---------|------------------|\n| **Skill** | A workflow with steps and exit criteria | `code-review-and-quality` | The *how* — invoked from inside a persona or command |\n| **Persona** | A role with a perspective and an output format | `code-reviewer` | The *who* — adopts a viewpoint, produces a report |\n| **Command** | A user-facing entry point | `/review`, `/ship` | The *when* — composes personas and skills |\n\nThe user (or a slash command) is the orchestrator. **Personas do not call other personas.** Skills are mandatory hops inside a persona's workflow.\n\n## When to use each\n\n### Direct persona invocation\nPick this when you want one perspective on the current change and the user is in the loop.\n\n- \"Review this PR\" → invoke `code-reviewer` directly\n- \"Are there security issues in `auth.ts`?\" → invoke `security-auditor` directly\n- \"What tests are missing for the checkout flow?\" → invoke `test-engineer` directly\n\n### Slash command (single persona behind it)\nPick this when there's a repeatable workflow you'd otherwise re-explain every time.\n\n- `/review` → wraps `code-reviewer` with the project's review skill\n- `/test` → wraps `test-engineer` with TDD skill\n\n### Slash command (orchestrator — fan-out)\nPick this only when **independent** investigations can run in parallel and produce reports that a single agent then merges.\n\n- `/ship` → fans out to `code-reviewer` + `security-auditor` + `test-engineer` in parallel, then synthesizes their reports into a go/no-go decision\n\nThis is the only orchestration pattern this repo endorses. See [references/orchestration-patterns.md](../references/orchestration-patterns.md) for the full pattern catalog and anti-patterns.\n\n## Decision matrix\n\n```\nIs the work a single perspective on a single artifact?\n├── Yes → Direct persona invocation\n└── No  → Are the sub-tasks independent (no shared mutable state, no ordering)?\n         ├── Yes → Slash command with parallel fan-out (e.g. /ship)\n         └── No  → Sequential slash commands run by the user (/spec → /plan → /build → /test → /review)\n```\n\n## Worked example: valid orchestration\n\n`/ship` is the canonical fan-out orchestrator in this repo:\n\n```\n/ship\n  ├── (parallel) code-reviewer    → review report\n  ├── (parallel) security-auditor → audit report\n  └── (parallel) test-engineer    → coverage report\n                  ↓\n        merge phase (main agent)\n                  ↓\n        go/no-go decision + rollback plan\n```\n\nWhy this works:\n- Each sub-agent operates on the same diff but produces a **different perspective**\n- They have no dependencies on each other → genuine parallelism, real wall-clock savings\n- Each runs in a fresh context window → main session stays uncluttered\n- The merge step is small and benefits from full context, so it stays in the main agent\n\n## Worked example: invalid orchestration (do not build this)\n\nA `meta-orchestrator` persona whose job is \"decide which other persona to call\":\n\n```\n/work-on-pr → meta-orchestrator\n                  ↓ (decides \"this needs a review\")\n              code-reviewer\n                  ↓ (returns)\n              meta-orchestrator (paraphrases result)\n                  ↓\n              user\n```\n\nWhy this fails:\n- Pure routing layer with no domain value\n- Adds two paraphrasing hops → information loss + 2× token cost\n- The user already knows they want a review; let them call `/review` directly\n- Replicates work that slash commands and `AGENTS.md` intent-mapping already do\n\n## Rules for personas\n\n1. A persona is a single role with a single output format. If you find yourself adding a second role, create a second persona.\n2. **Personas do not invoke other personas.** Composition is the job of slash commands or the user.
